findings.title: [P1] Reject non-finite timeout values instead of returning them
findings.body: `Number.isFinite` is `false` for `NaN` and `±Infinity`, so `if (Number.isFinite(timeout) && (...)) throw` skips the throw for exactly the invalid inputs. `parseTimeout("abc")` now returns `NaN` and `parseTimeout("Infinity")` returns `Infinity`, where the old `parseInt`-based code threw `invalid timeout` for both. Downstream, `NaN` is typically coerced to a `0` delay (`setTimeout`-style APIs) rather than surfacing an error. Correct form: `if (!Number.isFinite(timeout) || !Number.isSafeInteger(timeout) || timeout <= 0) throw ...`.

findings.title: [P2] Number() changes the accepted string formats vs the parseInt contract
findings.body: Beyond the non-finite bug, `Number(value)` vs `Number.parseInt(value, 10)` changes observable results: `"5.5"` previously returned `5` (silent truncation) and now throws; `"0x10"` previously threw and now returns `16`; `"1e3"` previously returned `1` and now returns `1000`. Tightening fractional input is defensible, but accepting hex/exponent notation is a widening that contradicts the PR's "preserving existing contracts" claim — confirm these format changes are intended.
